title: Dispersion and Scattering of Light
summary: ## Refraction through a prism
A ray passing through a prism of angle A is bent towards the base. The angles are related by r₁ + r₂ = A and the deviation δ = i + e − A.

As the angle of incidence increases, δ first decreases, reaches a minimum D_m and then increases (a U-shaped δ–i graph). At minimum deviation i = e, r = A/2 and the ray inside travels parallel to the base, so D_m = 2i − A.
μ = sin[(A + D_m)/2] / sin(A/2).
Examples: A = 60° and D_m = 39° give μ = sin 49.5°/sin 30° = 0.760/0.5 = 1.52. If D_m = A, then μ = 2 cos(A/2); for μ = √3, A = 60°. A = 60° with minimum deviation at i = 52° gives D_m = 44°.
A thin prism deviates light by δ = (μ − 1)A. For A = ½° and μ = 1.7, δ = 0.35°.
Prism in a liquid: use the relative refractive index μ_glass/μ_liquid, so the deviation becomes smaller.
## Dispersion

Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its colours (VIBGYOR), because μ depends on wavelength: μ is greatest for violet, which is deviated most, and least for red. A convex lens has a shorter focal length for violet or blue light, which therefore focuses nearest to it.
Angular dispersion θ = δ_v − δ_r = (μ_v − μ_r)A; it increases with the prism angle, so a larger-angled prism disperses more.
Dispersive power ω = (μ_v − μ_r)/(μ − 1) depends only on the material, not on the angle of the prism. Flint glass has a higher ω than crown glass, so it gives the broadest spectrum.
A glass slab does not disperse white light: its faces are parallel, so the colours emerge parallel and overlap again.
Ordinary gases show almost no dispersion because their refractive index is nearly 1 for all colours.
## Rainbow

A rainbow forms by dispersion together with refraction and total internal reflection in raindrops. The primary bow (one reflection, red outside) is narrower and brighter than the secondary (two reflections, colours reversed).
## Scattering
Rayleigh's law: the intensity of scattered light I ∝ 1/λ⁴, so blue scatters much more than red, and green more than red.

The sky looks blue because scattered blue light reaches us from all directions. The rising or setting sun looks red because light travels through more air and the blue is scattered out. From space or a satellite there is no air to scatter light, so the sky looks black.
## Raman effect

When monochromatic light is scattered by molecules, the scattered light contains the original frequency (the Rayleigh line) plus weaker lines of changed frequency (Raman lines), discovered by C. V. Raman in 1928 (Nobel Prize, 1930).

Stokes lines have a lower frequency (longer λ): the photon gives energy to the molecule. Anti-Stokes lines have a higher frequency: the photon takes energy from an already excited molecule. The shift equals the molecule's vibrational energy, so it is used to study molecular structure.

or: What is dispersion of light? Would you prefer a small-angled or a large-angled prism to produce dispersion?
Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its colours because μ varies with wavelength. A large-angled prism, since angular dispersion (μ_v − μ_r)A increases with the angle A.

Why do most ordinary gases not show dispersion of white light?
Their refractive index is very close to 1 and almost the same for all colours, so the colours are hardly separated.
Which of red and green light scatters more, and why?
Green, because scattering ∝ 1/λ⁴ and green has the shorter wavelength.
Name two phenomena based on scattering of light.
(1) The blue colour of the sky. (2) The red colour of the sun at sunrise and sunset. (Also the white colour of clouds.)

or: When monochromatic light is scattered by molecules, the scattered light contains, besides the original frequency, weaker lines of slightly lower and higher frequencies (Stokes and anti-Stokes lines).

sa: What is the Raman effect? How is the Raman spectrum produced? Explain Stokes and anti-Stokes lines.

Raman effect: when monochromatic light is scattered by a transparent substance, the scattered light contains the incident frequency ν plus new weaker frequencies ν ± Δν.
Photons collide inelastically with molecules. A photon giving energy to a molecule leaves with lower frequency — a Stokes line (ν − Δν). A photon taking energy from an excited molecule leaves with higher frequency — an anti-Stokes line (ν + Δν), weaker because few molecules are excited.
Δν matches the molecule's vibrational energy levels.
A glass prism of angle 60° and μ = 1.5 is immersed in water (μ = 1.33). Find the angle of minimum deviation. (sin⁻¹ 0.56 = 34.3°)

Relative index μ' = 1.5/1.33 ≈ 1.128.
sin[(A + D_m)/2] = μ' sin(A/2) = 1.128 × 0.5 = 0.564 ≈ 0.56.
(A + D_m)/2 = 34.3° ⇒ A + D_m = 68.6° ⇒ D_m ≈ 8.6°.
The deviation in water is much less than in air (about 37°).
Explain why (i) the sky appears blue from the earth and dark from space and (ii) the sun appears red at sunrise.

(i) Air molecules scatter sunlight with I ∝ 1/λ⁴, so blue is scattered most and reaches our eyes from all parts of the sky. In space there is no atmosphere to scatter light, so the sky looks dark.
(ii) At sunrise sunlight crosses a long path through the air. Most blue light is scattered away, and the remaining light reaching us is reddish.
Write the expression for dispersive power. How does the width of a spectrum depend on (i) dispersive power and (ii) the angle of the prism? Why is flint glass preferred?

ω = (μ_v − μ_r)/(μ − 1); angular dispersion θ = ωδ = (μ_v − μ_r)A.
(i) The width of the spectrum increases with ω.
(ii) It increases with the prism angle A.
Flint glass has a higher dispersive power than crown glass, so it gives a wider spectrum.
la: Define the angle of minimum deviation. Draw the graph between the angle of deviation and the angle of incidence. A 60° prism has minimum deviation A/2; find μ. Derive μ = sin[(A + D_m)/2]/sin(A/2).

The angle of minimum deviation is the smallest deviation produced by a prism, when the ray passes through symmetrically (i = e, ray parallel to the base).
Graph: δ falls as i increases, reaches D_m, then rises (U-shaped curve).
Derivation: r₁ + r₂ = A and δ = i + e − A. At minimum deviation r₁ = r₂ = A/2 and i = e = (A + D_m)/2. Snell's law gives μ = sin i/sin r = sin[(A + D_m)/2]/sin(A/2).
For A = 60°, D_m = 30°: μ = sin 45°/sin 30° = √2 ≈ 1.41.
A ray of white light splits into its colours on passing through a glass prism but not through a glass slab. Explain with diagrams.

In a prism the two refracting faces are inclined. Each colour has a different μ, so it is deviated by a different amount and the colours spread out — violet most, red least — forming a spectrum.
In a slab the faces are parallel. Each colour is bent at the first face and bent back equally at the second, so all colours emerge parallel to the incident ray, only slightly displaced. They overlap again and the light looks white.
